item.title: Gold erases gains as Nvidia optimism fades and US moves to restore tariffs to 2025 levels
item.description:
Gold erased all the weekly gains yesterday as the market optimism from Nvidia news faded rather quickly. The catalyst seemed to be the WSJ report saying that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

After the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025.

According to the Financial Times, the US is expected to honour previous trade agreements by capping the new tariffs for countries that had negotiated deals with the Trump administration. Overall, this isn’t a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

For gold, it’s a tricky situation because it keeps getting smashed lower when the stock market falls on growth concerns and the gains are capped when the sentiment improves because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. But buyers will also need to be aware that a dovish repricing from renewed stock market selloff could lead to more liquidations.

 

GOLD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

We can expect the buyers to step in around the 3,500 level, with a defined risk below it, to position for a rally into the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to target the 3,100 level next.

item.title: France November consumer confidence improves slightly but economic worries persist
item.description:
• France November consumer confidence 82 vs 82 expeccted
  • Prior 80; revised to 81

Despite a mild improvement to October, French household confidence remains subdued for the most part and continues to hold well below the long-term average of 100.

The November survey was a mixed one with some improvements seen in sub-categories for the expected financial situation, standard of living, unemployment prospects, as well as some easing in inflation concerns. However, there were some slight softening in the likes of current and expected saving capacity, and major purchase intentions. Of note, the savings climate synthetic index fell to its lowest since August 2024.

So, this is not to say that things are looking on the up in France as we look to end the year.

Having said that, households' fears about unemployment have fallen back in November and that is a good thing. But even with the sub-index at 54, it is still well above what we saw in January at 47. So, the impact of the relative uncertainty caused by geopolitical and fiscal worries is still very much weighing.

Perhaps the most notable thing for the ECB is that the proportion of households who consider that prices will accelerate over the next twelve months has fallen back sharply. The measure of future inflation fell back from -8 in October to -17 in November, moving closer to its long-term average.

Overall, this will do little to distract from the fact that France remains Europe's biggest headache at the moment. And the ECB will need little reminder of that ahead of their final meeting decision in December, in which they hope to still at least be able to get away with one more rate hike to end the year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What are the main events for today?
item.description:
EUROPEAN SESSION

In the European session, we don't have much on the agenda other than a couple of low-tier releases like the final German GDP report and the French Consumer Confidence. The data won't change anything for the ECB, so the market reaction will likely be muted. As a reminder, the ECB is widely expected to hike by 25 bps at the December meeting. The market then expects another rate hike in June 2027. 

AMERICAN SESSION

In the American session, we get the second estimate of the US Q3 GDP, the US Durable Goods Orders, the US Core PCE price index and the US Jobless Claims figures. The US GDP is going to be ignored. It's old data since we are almost at the end of Q4, and it won't change anything for the Fed given its focus on inflation. The US Durable Goods Orders data is never a market-moving release because it's very volatile and doesn't give any real signal. 

The US PCE price index is rarely a major market-moving event because it can be forecasted fairly accurately using inputs from the CPI, PPI and Import prices. That's why the US CPI moves the markets the most as the PCE becomes old news by the time it's released. The PCE Y/Y is expected at 3.8% vs 3.6% prior, while the M/M measure is seen at 0.3% vs 0.5% prior. The Core PCE Y/Y is expected at 3.2% vs 3.1% prior, while the M/M figure is seen at 0.3% vs 0.3% prior.

The only important data is going to be the US Jobless Claims. This is because growth concerns became the primary focus for the market amid a more hawkish Fed, AI selloff, prolonged US-Iran stalemate, widening credit spreads, Democratic Congress... well, you get the idea. Jobless Claims provide the timeliest view on the US labour market conditions. Initial Claims are expected at 200K vs 203K prior, while Continuing Claims are seen at 1740K vs 1763K prior.

item.title: German economy flirts with stagnation in Q3 as growth is revised lower
item.description:
• Germany Q3 final GDP +0.1% vs +0.2% q/q prelim
  • Prior +0.3%
  • Germany Q3 final GDP +1.1% vs +1.2% y/y prelim
  • Prior +1.0%

The revision lower reaffirms that the German economy nearly stagnated in Q3, as economic growth slowed after the more resilient showing in the first half of the year. The toll from the geopolitical crisis in the Middle East is still being exerted and the impact is still making its way across the European economy in general.

Looking at the details, consumer spending showed slight growth (+0.1%) on the quarter while equipment investment is significantly down (-3.5%). Private consumption, which accounts for about 70% of total consumption expenditure, rose by 0.1%. Meanwhile, gross fixed capital formation fell by 1.2% on the quarter.

Besides that, the trade mix also changed compared to what we saw in the first half of the year. Exports fell by 1.0% on the quarter while imports fell by 1.4% on the quarter. The breakdown notably shows a sharp fall in service exports (-1.7%) but there were also declines in exports of motor vehicles and motor vehicle parts, chemical products, and metals.

Overall, this points to some moderation in growth conditions in Europe's largest economy in Q3 after a decent showing in Q1 and Q2 despite the challenges from the US-Iran conflict. The preliminary hard data for Q4 suggests that things should continue to hold up as well to round off the year, so that will at least afford the ECB some breathing room in their battle against inflation.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold is losing its grip again as sellers eye a break of the $3,500 level
item.description:
That didn't last very long, did it?

After an early bounce on Monday, gold stumbled in trading yesterday and is down another 1% today and we're already staring at another test of the $3,500 mark. The precious metal is on course for a third straight weekly decline and its sixth in seven weeks. Ouch.

As much as the selling pressures might seem excessive, the fact of the matter is that not much has changed from a technical standpoint this week.

The break below the 100-week moving average (red line) just under $4,000 remains the elephant in the room. That was the first serious breach of the key technical level since 2023 and has disrupted the upside momentum in gold that has helped to sustain the stunning rally for much of the last two years.

As seen with the chart above, what looks to be alarming is that if $3,500 gives way, there isn't much in the way of any major technical support until the $3,000-$3,140 region. That's where the 200-week moving average (blue line) and the 61.8 Fib retracement level of the broader rally come into play. That suggests there is quite a bit of air underneath the current price level.

And as mentioned yesterday, I still like the long-term story for gold. However, there's a difference between liking the asset proposition and liking the trade that is right in front of you. Even if gold is at the cheapest levels for this year, it doesn't mean that it is time to go bargain hunting just yet.

"That's not something that will likely be fixed by a couple of good days on Wall Street. For now, the tug of war is back on. However, I'd much rather pay a little more for gold with some technical conviction behind the recovery than get caught up trying to catch a falling knife at the moment."

In essence, dip buyers have to prove that they have staying power above $3,500 for an extended period to even be taken seriously at this point. Otherwise, it feels like it is only a matter of time before the next wave of selling hits and we go in search of the next ledge for gold to try and hang on to.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: No Thanksgiving cheer for markets as Europe gets set for another nervy session
item.description:
Well, it was fun while it lasted, eh? After all the excitement surrounding Wall Street's rebound on Monday, we're back to some rather familiar territory heading into European trading today.

The selloff in US tech stocks is resuming and there isn't much appetite to pick up the pieces just yet. After the drop yesterday, S&P 500 futures are now down another 0.8% while Nasdaq futures are down 1.4% currently. So much for Jensen Huang coming to the rescue.

And just to make things a little more uncomfortable for investors, US president Trump is stirring the tariffs pot again. Oh, how fun.

But even without that, there are enough questions surrounding AI spending, stretched valuations and elevated Treasury yields to keep broader markets on their toes. And that has been the case for a few weeks already now.

So, what can we extrapolate from the market mood in the past few sessions?

The most telling thing is how quickly the enthusiasm from Monday has evaporated. The appetite for dip buying folded with sellers regaining control without much of a fight. So, that is the key takeaway for me.

Over in the major currencies space, the dollar continues to keep firmer as well on the week. The early mover today though was the aussie as it had something to cheer about after another hot inflation report out of Australia. Trimmed mean inflation jumped to 3.8% in October, keeping the prospect of further RBA rate hikes alive. AUD/USD got a decent bump from that to 0.6660 but has since given back those gains and then some to 0.6590 now.

So, where does all this leave us with heading into European trading later?

Well, it's back to the same playbook as it has been all week I guess. Unless we get a fresh catalyst during the session, European traders might find themselves taking their cues from Wall Street once again.

All eyes will be on the risk selloff and we're already seeing a more risk-off mood start to take hold. So, that will make for a bit of an ugly start to the morning in Europe.

And with Thanksgiving coming tomorrow, do be mindful of thinner liquidity conditions in the second half of the week. With fewer traders around, even relatively modest orders can result in exacerbated price swings in market action.

As such, I'd be wary of chasing any sharp rebounds under those circumstances. It's as good a time to be reminded that a sudden jump in stocks amid thinner holiday liquidity isn't quite the same thing as investors rediscovering their conviction to buy.

As things stand, I would argue that the bulls might have to wait a little longer for their Thanksgiving feast. For now, it's the bears who are being served seconds.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Japan looks to ease fiscal fears as Takaichi seeks to avoid fresh deficit bonds
item.description:
A little less borrowing and a little more fiscal discipline? That's probably something that yen traders wouldn't mind hearing from Tokyo.

The latest headlines from TBS is reporting that Japan prime minister Takaichi and her administration is planning to avoid issuing new deficit-financing bonds for this fiscal year's supplementary budget. Now, just be mindful that this has been rumoured for a few weeks already. So, the latest headlines are just adding to that.

However, what is interesting is that this follows from the government's draft budget guidelines yesterday, which emphasised fiscal sustainability and the need to maintain market confidence. So, it seems very much that the fiscal conversation in Japan is now as much about managing market expectations as it is about supporting economic growth.

Since taking over as prime minister, Takaichi's expansionary fiscal agenda has been a sticking point for Japanese markets. The Takaichi trade has been a major bane for the yen as traders had to contend with the prospect of more government spending, persistent inflation and higher borrowing costs all at once.

So, how does this latest development change things?

Well, avoiding fresh deficit-financing bonds would help alleviate concerns about additional debt supply. However, let's not jump the gun and confuse that with a step towards fiscal tightening. The government can still increase spending by tapping other sources of revenue and that could still have implications for inflation.

Now, where does that leave the BOJ then?

In a perfect world, greater fiscal discipline should make it easier for the BOJ to raise interest rates without causing too much distress in the bond market. But hey, we're not living in a perfect world. If fiscal spending remains expansionary for the most part, the central bank might still find itself having to work harder to contain inflation.

As such, therein lies the awkward relationship between fiscal and monetary policy in Japan right now. Tokyo wants to support the economy through spending while the BOJ is trying to gradually take away the monetary stimulus that has supported it for years. So until traders see a more convincing alignment between Japan's fiscal and monetary policies, I wouldn't expect the yen's fortunes to change on one small step in the right direction.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Equities

item.title: UBS sees gold at $5,000 by end-2027, well above Goldman's $4,650 call
item.description:
A $5,000 target from a major wealth manager strengthens the long-term bull case for gold, but UBS's own list of headwinds is a reminder that the near-term path runs through the Fed. With US policy on a hiking path and the dollar firm, gold remains sensitive to every shift in rate expectations, including Wednesday's PCE inflation data. Any sign that Fed tightening is nearing its end would likely be the trigger for gold to start closing the gap toward bank forecasts. Steady central bank buying offers a floor of demand, which helps explain why forecasters remain confident on the 2027 outlook despite this year's weakness.

---

UBS is sticking with gold, forecasting $5,000 an ounce by end-2027 on central bank demand and debt worries, even as higher US real yields and a strong dollar keep the metal under pressure for now.

Summary:

  • UBS keeps gold at Attractive and forecasts $5,000 an ounce by December 2027
  • It cites central bank reserve diversification, sovereign debt, geopolitical uncertainty and Chinese demand as supports
  • UBS acknowledges that higher US real yields, dollar strength and liquidity-driven selling are weighing on prices
  • Goldman Sachs forecasts $4,650 by end-2027, and CIBC sees $5,200 in 2027
  • UBS frames gold as part of broader diversification, alongside commodities including copper
  • The timing of any rally is likely to hinge on when US rate expectations peak

UBS Global Wealth Management has reaffirmed its constructive view on gold, keeping the metal rated Attractive and forecasting that it will reach $5,000 an ounce by December 2027. The call, set out in a note on portfolio positioning after a volatile stretch for markets, implies a gain of more than a third from the level of around $3,600 referenced in the note, and places UBS toward the top of the major banks' forecasts.

The bank sees gold's role as strategic rather than tactical. It points to four lasting supports: continued diversification of central bank reserves away from traditional holdings, high and rising sovereign debt, persistent geopolitical uncertainty, and demand from China. Together, UBS argues, these give the metal a place in portfolios as a source of return that does not depend on the same drivers as stocks and bonds.

UBS is also clear about what has been holding gold back. Higher US real yields, a strong dollar and liquidity-driven selling have all weighed on prices, and those pressures have been sharpened by the Federal Reserve's return to rate increases this year. Gold has struggled through much of 2026 as markets priced a higher path for US interest rates, and its moves have often tracked rate expectations more closely than geopolitical headlines.

The UBS target stands out against recent calls from other banks. Goldman Sachs expects gold to climb back above $4,600 and reach $4,650 by the end of 2027, arguing that structural central bank buying will eventually win out even as higher rate expectations slow the metal in the near term. CIBC cut its forecast for the current quarter to $4,500 last month but sees a rebound to $5,200 in 2027. The common thread is that central bank demand underpins the long-term case, while the timing depends heavily on the Fed.

For UBS, gold sits alongside a broader push for diversification. The bank argues that in a world where government policy increasingly drives economic outcomes and market leadership is concentrated in a small number of large technology companies, investors should spread their sources of return more widely. It also sees a role for diversified commodity exposure, including copper, to help portfolios cope with inflation, geopolitical shocks, climate disruption and supply risks.

The path to $5,000 is likely to depend on when US rate expectations peak. A pause in Fed tightening, or a turn lower in real yields and the dollar, would remove the main obstacles UBS has identified, while continued central bank purchases provide a steady source of demand in the meantime.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Four ways to own gold, and the new one JPMorgan and HSBC just tested in London
item.description:
The pilot changes how gold is held and moved, not how much investors want, so it has little bearing on prices near term. Spot gold remains under pressure from near-certain expectations of a December Fed hike and sits not far above last week's more-than-one-year low. The longer-term effect could be supportive. Gold that can be pledged as collateral in real time earns a role on institutional balance sheets beyond being a store of value. For crypto, the pilot adds institutional competition to on-chain gold tokens such as XAUT and PAXG. It also gives regulators a working wholesale model to point to as the FCA shapes its rules for tokenised gold.

---

Earlier:

  • How crypto loans unwind: what a $43.8 million ether sale teaches about leverage

---

Gold has always been trusted and hard to move; London's biggest dealers have now tested a way to keep the trust and lose some of the weight.

Summary:

  • The World Gold Council said on November 24 that JPMorgan, HSBC and StoneX had completed the first live, legally binding trades using Pooled Gold Interests (PGIs).
  • The firms traded, settled and used fractional ownership of physical bars as collateral, with no metal leaving the vault.
  • ICE Benchmark Administration operates the system and Baton Systems provides the settlement technology. The WGC release doesn't say it runs on a blockchain.
  • PGIs aim to combine the legal ownership of allocated gold with the flexibility of unallocated gold.
  • The two largest on-chain gold tokens hold about 1.27 million ounces, well under 1% of London's vaulted gold.
  • The pilot has no launch date. The FCA is preparing a wider Tokenisation Roadmap.

JPMorgan, HSBC and StoneX have completed the first live, legally binding trades in a new form of gold ownership in London, the World Gold Council said on November 24. The three firms traded and settled fractional ownership interests in physical gold bars, and used those interests as collateral, without moving any metal out of the vault.

The structure is called a Pooled Gold Interest (PGI), and it is still at pilot stage. But it targets one of the oldest frictions in the bullion market: gold is valuable, trusted and heavy, and the last of those makes it awkward to use. To see why the PGI matters, it helps to understand the three main ways gold is already held, and where the new option sits between them.

Why gold needs new plumbing

The London market runs on 400-ounce Good Delivery bars. London vaults held about 9,850 tonnes of gold at the end of October, according to LBMA monthly data. The World Gold Council puts over-the-counter trading in the city at more than $180 billion a day.

Almost none of that trading involves bars changing hands. Moving a bar means insuring it, transporting it and recording it, and a single bar is worth around $1.4 million at current prices. So most of the market trades claims on gold rather than gold itself. Each ownership model answers the same two questions differently: what exactly do you own, and what happens if the institution holding it fails?

1. Allocated gold

What you own: specific, numbered bars, held in your name and kept separate from the custodian's own assets.

The trade-off: this is the safest form of ownership, because the bars are yours if the custodian goes bust. But bars can't be split, and transferring ownership is slow and costly.

2. Unallocated gold

What you own: a claim on a bullion bank for a quantity of gold, backed by the bank's general pool of metal.

The trade-off: unallocated accounts carry most of London's trading because they're flexible. Any amount can be traded and settled without touching a bar. The catch is that the holder is a creditor of the bank, not the owner of any metal. If the bank fails, the holder joins the queue.

3. Pooled Gold Interests

What you own: a proprietary interest in a pool of segregated physical bars, transferred electronically.

The trade-off: the PGI tries to combine the strengths of the first two models. Like allocated gold, it is ownership rather than a claim on a bank. Like unallocated gold, it can be split into fractions and moved quickly. In the pilot, bars were placed into the system, interests were created, traded and settled, and the gold was then withdrawn to complete the cycle. Mark Amlin, JPMorgan's global head of physical commodities, said gold ownership that is fractional, readily transferable and "insolvency remote" would let gold be used more widely, including as collateral.

ICE Benchmark Administration operates the system and Baton Systems provides the settlement technology. Notably, the World Gold Council's announcement describes a real-time settlement layer and does not say the system runs on a blockchain.

4. On-chain gold tokens

What you own: a crypto token, such as Tether Gold (XAUT) or Paxos's PAX Gold (PAXG), each representing one troy ounce of physical gold held by the issuer.

The trade-off: tokens trade around the clock on public blockchains, and anyone with a crypto wallet can buy them in small amounts. Holders depend on the issuer's custody, redemption terms and legal jurisdiction. The two largest tokens held about 1.27 million ounces combined, roughly 39.5 tonnes, up 48% from a year earlier, according to a Coinspeaker analysis of their on-chain supply. That growth is fast, but the total is still well under 1% of the gold sitting in London's vaults.

Why collateral is the real prize

Trading is the headline, but the collateral test is the bigger step. Banks and funds constantly pledge assets to back derivatives, repo and other borrowing. Gold is already accepted for some of these uses, but because it's hard to move, much of it sits idle while cash and government bonds do the work.

A structure that lets institutions pledge part of a bar in real time, while keeping clear legal ownership, could turn vaulted gold into working collateral. UK regulators have flagged the same opportunity. The Financial Conduct Authority closed a Call for Input on tokenised gold in October, with collateral as a central use case, and has said it expects to publish a wider Tokenisation Roadmap later this year.

There is a competitive angle too. Bloomberg framed the pilot as an effort to keep London ahead of Asian hubs. According to Coinspeaker, Hong Kong has been testing a gold clearing system with the Shanghai Gold Exchange since July.

What it means for the gold price

Not much in the short run. The pilot changes how gold is held and moved, not how much of it investors want. Spot gold traded around $3,545 an ounce on Wednesday in Asia, Reuters reported. That followed a fall of more than 2% on Tuesday and a low last Friday that was the weakest since September 2025. Markets are pricing roughly a 96% chance of a Fed rate hike in December, which raises the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest. According to Reuters, Goldman Sachs analysts expect the downward pressure to eventually reverse, though possibly more slowly around year-end.

Over a longer horizon, the case is structural. If gold becomes easier to pledge, institutions have one more reason to hold it, because it would no longer have to sit idle. That is a demand argument measured in years, not sessions.

What to watch next

Next steps on the pilot: the World Gold Council has not set a launch date. More participants, especially other London clearing banks and custodians, would show whether this becomes market infrastructure or stays a three-firm trial.

The FCA's Tokenisation Roadmap: how it treats tokenised gold, including whether some products fall under fund rules, will shape who can use these structures and how.

On-chain token supply: continued growth in XAUT and PAXG would show retail and crypto demand for gold moving on-chain alongside the institutional version.

Near term: the October PCE inflation report, due later on Wednesday in the US, will matter more for the gold price, through its effect on Fed hike expectations.

What could change the reading: a smooth rollout with wide participation would make the PGI one of the biggest changes to London's bullion market in decades. A stalled pilot, or rules that limit its use as collateral, would leave it as an interesting experiment and leave on-chain tokens as the main route to fractional gold. 

--- 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Asian stocks slide as AI doubts return, Kospi down nearly 6% and Nikkei more than 3%
item.description:
The renewed slide in Asia's chip giants shows how fragile Monday's AI relief rally was, and keeps pressure on the most crowded technology positions heading into a potentially holiday-thinned US session. Safer assets drew modest support: Japanese government bond yields eased despite Wednesday's hot services inflation data, and the yen held near 159 per dollar. Oil extended its slide, with Brent near $88 and WTI around $81, as risk aversion weighed alongside supply concerns. The Australian dollar slipped to around 66.2 US cents despite the stronger-than-expected CPI. Gold was little changed near $3,560 an ounce.

---

The AI trade stumbled again in Asia, with chipmakers dragging the Kospi and Nikkei sharply lower and US futures extending losses ahead of a crowded day of US data.

Summary:

  • The Kospi fell nearly 6%, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both down more than 8%
  • Foreign investors were net sellers, and analysts cited profit-taking and tariff concerns
  • The Nikkei 225 dropped more than 3%, while the broader TOPIX fell about 1%
  • Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose about 1%, while Shanghai eased slightly
  • Nasdaq 100 futures fell about 1% and S&P 500 futures about 0.5%
  • US PCE inflation, GDP and jobless claims are due at 13:30 GMT ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday

Asian equities came under heavy pressure on Wednesday as an overnight slump in US technology shares revived doubts about the artificial intelligence trade, wiping out much of the relief rally seen earlier in the week. Chip stocks bore the brunt of the selling, with South Korea and Japan among the hardest-hit markets.

South Korea's Kospi fell close to 6% to around 4,710 by mid-afternoon, as heavyweight chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each dropped more than 8%. Foreign investors were net sellers, Reuters reported, and analysts pointed to profit-taking after Tuesday's sharp rebound, along with concern over the possibility of additional US tariffs. The smaller Kosdaq lost close to 3%.

Japan's Nikkei 225 slid more than 3% to around 56,660, as the regional selloff in technology shares spread to Tokyo. The broader TOPIX held up better, down about 1% at around 3,730, reflecting its larger weighting toward financials and domestically focused companies.

Elsewhere, China's Shanghai Composite eased slightly less than 1%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng bucked the regional trend to gain about 1%.

The selling followed weeks of volatility in AI-related stocks, as investors questioned the debt-funded spending behind the sector and the returns it is likely to generate. Monday's rebound, sparked by the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive, briefly eased those concerns, but the mood soured again as Wall Street's technology names gave back ground on Tuesday.

US index futures extended losses during the Asian session, with Nasdaq 100 futures down about 1%, S&P 500 futures off roughly half a percent and Dow futures slightly lower.

Attention now turns to a busy US session, with October's personal consumption expenditures price index (preview), the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, due at 13:30 GMT alongside revised third-quarter GDP data and weekly jobless claims. With US markets closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, thinner trading ahead could amplify any moves.

item.title: Goldman sees TOPIX up 20% to 4,500 and names five themes for Japanese stocks in 2027
item.description:
Goldman's call hinges on continued global AI spending, which leaves Japanese stocks exposed to the same AI-funding doubts that have hit US technology shares this month. The expected broadening could favour mid-cap restructuring candidates, trading houses, shippers and energy firms over the crowded AI and bank trades that led this year. A steady flow of takeover bids and buyouts would add a deal premium across the market. On the macro side, further Bank of Japan hikes, made more likely by Wednesday's hot services inflation reading, would lift the yen and could weigh on exporters. It would, however, support the banks' earnings base.

---

Goldman Sachs expects another strong year for Japanese stocks, with the TOPIX seen at 4,500, but says the rally should rely less on AI and banks and more on restructuring, robotics, energy security and a government push for companies to spend.

Summary:

  • Goldman projects the TOPIX rising about 20% to 4,500 over the next 12 months, with EPS growth of 9% in fiscal 2027
  • Gains depend on continued AI capital spending, and 2027 is seen as a transitional year
  • Tokyo's regulators and government are pushing firms to use excess cash for growth
  • Goldman expects a significant rise in takeover bids, buyouts and consolidation from 2027
  • Its five themes are AI innovation and quality, corporate restructuring, physical AI, energy and resource security, and cybersecurity
  • Energy security projects overlap with the $550 billion US-Japan trade deal

Japanese stocks are set to rally again over the coming year, but the drivers of the gains are likely to change, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The bank's strategists project the TOPIX index will rise about 20% to 4,500 over the next 12 months, based on forecasts for earnings per share growth of 9% in fiscal 2027, as long as global spending on artificial intelligence continues.

Bruce Kirk, Goldman's chief Japan equity strategist, describes 2027 as a transitional year for the market. Gains over the past three years have been driven mainly by AI-related stocks, banks and the Bank of Japan's move away from ultra-loose policy. Kirk expects the rally to broaden as investors diversify into less crowded and less volatile themes, and as the government steps up efforts to get companies to put their cash to work.

That policy push is coordinated across Tokyo. Kirk points to a consistent message from the Tokyo Stock Exchange, the Financial Services Agency, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's administration, all encouraging firms to use excess cash reserves to fund future growth. Japan's revised corporate governance code now emphasises growth-oriented governance and fair treatment of minority shareholders in mergers.

Goldman argues that lifting the TOPIX's return on equity, which still lags many global markets, will require more forceful restructuring than has occurred so far, including mergers, segment overhauls and sector consolidation. It expects a significant rise in takeover bids, management buyouts and industry consolidation from 2027.

Kirk identifies five themes for investors. The first is AI innovation and quality, with higher-quality AI-related companies having outperformed their peers. The second is corporate restructuring. The third is physical AI: labour costs for non-financial TOPIX companies rose to 10.5% of sales in fiscal 2025, a decade high, while Goldman expects humanoid robot prices to halve to about $21,000 by 2035, and the government is targeting 350,000 AI robots by 2030. The fourth is energy and resource security. Japan imports almost all of its oil, gas, coal and critical minerals, and its energy self-sufficiency, at 16% in 2024, remains low. Government plans to diversify supply and expand solar, thermal and advanced nuclear power could benefit trading houses, shipping firms, energy companies and heavy industry, with overlap seen with projects under the $550 billion US-Japan trade deal. The fifth is cybersecurity, where Tokyo wants domestic firms to reach annual revenue of more than 3 trillion yen by 2035.

The energy theme is already playing out. Japan this week agreed to buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its strategic reserve, while giving Riyadh more storage capacity on Japanese soil.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS: AI sell-off reflects a shift from spending to returns, not the end of the AI story
item.description:
UBS's framing suggests the AI shake-out is more likely to produce a widening gap between stronger and weaker names than a uniform sell-off. Companies relying on debt or temporarily scarce capacity are most exposed if financing conditions tighten further. With the Fed on a hiking path, that financing angle carries extra weight. A $5,000 gold target from a major wealth manager supports the long-term case for the metal, though UBS itself acknowledges that higher real yields and a firm dollar are near-term headwinds. Bond markets could also benefit if more investors rebuild fixed income allocations after years of equity outperformance.

---

Earlier:

  • JPMorgan's 8,200 S&P 500 target for 2027 sits below peers as Fed risk tempers AI upside
  • Deutsche Bank sees S&P 500 at 9,000 by end-2027, 25% upside on AI-driven earnings

---

UBS sees the AI sell-off as investors starting to demand returns on the spending boom, a shift that should reward cash-rich platforms over debt-dependent players, while it holds equities at Neutral and backs gold to reach $5,000.

Summary:

  • UBS says market focus has shifted from the scale of AI spending to the returns it may generate
  • The structural AI case is intact, supported by cloud growth, rising usage and demand for computing capacity
  • UBS expects a sharper divide between cash-generating platforms with strong balance sheets and debt-reliant or speculative players
  • Global and US equities stay at Neutral, which UBS says means holding allocations steady, not selling
  • UBS favours gradual rebalancing, broader diversification and rebuilding fixed income holdings
  • Gold is kept at Attractive, with a forecast of $5,000 an ounce by December 2027

The recent turbulence in technology stocks marks a change in what investors are asking of artificial intelligence rather than a collapse of the investment story behind it, according to UBS Global Wealth Management. Its strategists argue that attention has moved from the sheer scale of AI capital spending to the returns that spending might generate, and that this shift is likely to separate winners from losers more sharply in the months ahead.

UBS does not see the volatility as a sign that the structural case for AI has broken. Cloud growth, rising usage and continued demand for computing capacity all remain supportive, in its view. What it does expect is greater differentiation. Established platforms that can already show how they make money from AI, with strong balance sheets and the ability to fund investment from their own cash, are seen on firmer ground than companies that depend on debt, on capacity that is scarce for now, or on continued speculative growth.

The bank's stance on equities had already turned more measured before the latest bout of volatility. It keeps global and US equities at Neutral, citing elevated expectations, highly concentrated market leadership and growing uncertainty over how AI will be monetised. UBS stresses that this is not a call to sell stocks, but to hold exposure broadly in line with long-term allocations rather than leaning further in.

A wider theme runs through the note. In a world where government policy increasingly shapes economic outcomes and AI capacity is concentrated in a handful of large companies, UBS argues that the future cannot be read from market forces alone, making diversification across sources of return more important. It favours gradual, disciplined rebalancing over all-or-nothing bets on short-term market direction, and sees a case for many portfolios to rebuild fixed income holdings after several strong years for equities, with elevated starting yields offering both income and a cushion.

Gold remains a core part of that picture. UBS keeps the metal rated Attractive and forecasts it will reach $5,000 an ounce by December 2027.

Before changing its tactical view on equities, UBS will watch the pace of AI investment, demand for computing capacity, financing conditions, and whether revenues and free cash flow are keeping up with spending. Those measures are likely to decide whether the current shake-out proves a healthy reset or the start of something deeper.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Yen and euro both seen gaining on the dollar by end-2027, but on different paths
item.description:
Deutsche Bank's two calls point to opposite trades early in 2027. Its euro path favours the dollar in the first half, while its yen view argues against chasing USD/JPY higher from near 159, where the yen is pinned by a wide rate gap. For Japanese investors, any repatriation would also weigh on demand for US Treasuries and equities, adding to pressure on longer US yields. The euro rebound is tied to falling energy prices, so a renewed oil spike from Gulf disruption would be the main threat to that call. Both forecasts hinge on the Fed: tightening beyond the bank's assumed 75 basis points would delay any turn against the dollar.

--

Earlier:

  • Deutsche Bank sees S&P 500 at 9,000 by end-2027, 25% upside on AI-driven earnings

---

Deutsche Bank expects both the yen and the euro to end 2027 stronger against the dollar, but the yen's gain rests on Japanese money coming home while the euro first has to ride out a Fed-driven dollar surge.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank forecasts USD/JPY at 145 and EUR/USD at 1.15 by end-2027
  • The bank raised its dollar forecasts, citing AI-driven gains in US real rates and heavy equity inflows
  • The yen view rests on capital repatriation as Japanese yields rise, the BOJ hikes twice more to 1.75% and policy keeps savings at home
  • EUR/USD is seen falling to 1.08 in the first half on a further 75bp of Fed tightening, French political risk and ECB expectations
  • A euro recovery to 1.15 later in the year is tied to resilient European growth and Brent falling toward $70
  • The yen gain could come even if the dollar stays strong elsewhere, while the euro's turn depends on the cycle

Deutsche Bank expects both the yen and the euro to finish 2027 stronger against the US dollar, but it sees the two currencies taking very different routes there. In its 2027 World Outlook, the bank forecasts USD/JPY at 145 and EUR/USD at 1.15 by the end of next year. The yen's gain is expected to come largely from shifting capital flows, while the euro first has to ride out a period of dollar strength.

The forecasts sit within a broader upgrade to the bank's dollar view. Strategists including Tim Baker and George Saravelos said the artificial intelligence boom has pushed US real interest rates higher and drawn heavy foreign inflows into US equities, leaving the dollar unusually firm by historical standards. They now expect it to stay elevated for longer, with some strength in the first half of 2027 before a modest drift lower.

For the yen, the bank's argument is about money coming home. Higher Japanese bond yields, further Bank of Japan tightening and policies designed to keep domestic savings in Japan could reduce Japanese demand for US assets. Deutsche Bank expects two more BOJ hikes, taking the policy rate to 1.75%. It also notes that large Asian trade surpluses linked to the AI boom have been recycled into US markets, a pattern that could weaken. If repatriation builds, the yen could strengthen even while the dollar holds firm against other currencies. That would be a significant shift from current levels near 159 per dollar.

The euro story is about timing. Deutsche Bank expects the Federal Reserve to raise rates by another 75 basis points, taking its target range to 4.50% to 4.75%, which should keep the dollar strong into the first half of 2027. Combined with political uncertainty in France and expectations for the European Central Bank, that could push EUR/USD down to 1.08. The bank then sees a reversal to 1.15 by year-end, helped by resilient European growth and a fall in Brent crude toward $70 a barrel in the second half, which would ease the region's energy bill.

The contrast matters for positioning. The yen call depends on a structural change in how Japanese investors allocate savings, which could unfold regardless of the wider dollar trend. The euro call depends more on the economic cycle, with Fed policy and energy prices setting the pace. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman sees 9% return for European stocks as 2027 earnings growth slows to 7%
item.description:
Goldman's sensitivity estimate ties the outlook for European equities directly to oil: each 10% move in Brent shifts valuations by about 1%. That makes this week's slide in crude toward three-month lows a quiet tailwind for the region, and puts Hormuz headlines and Sunday's OPEC+ meeting on equity investors' radar as well. A falling energy bill would favour cyclicals, consumer names and the DAX over energy producers, defensives and the FTSE 100. Goldman's $78 end-2027 Brent call also sits well below Barclays' $85 forecast for 2027, a sign of how far apart the big banks are on the oil path.

---

Goldman Sachs expects European stocks to keep rising in 2027 but to lag the US and Asia as earnings growth slows, with cheaper energy the biggest potential tailwind and government debt the main drag.

Summary:

  • Goldman forecasts a 9% total return for the Stoxx 600 over the next 12 months, lagging the US and Asia
  • European earnings growth is expected to slow to 7% in 2027 from 18% this year
  • The valuation discount to US stocks has narrowed to about 14% on a sector-adjusted basis, from a peak of 34%
  • AI diversification, strong free cash flow and buybacks, and foreign inflows support allocations to Europe
  • Each 10% rise in Brent cuts European valuations by about 1%, and Goldman expects Brent to fall to $78 by end-2027
  • Goldman prefers Germany and UK domestic stocks and sees it as too early to return to French domestic stocks

European stocks are set to keep rising in 2027 but are likely to trail the US and Asia as earnings growth slows sharply, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The bank's strategists forecast a 9% total return for the Stoxx 600 over the next 12 months, with earnings growth expected to ease to 7% next year from 18% in 2026.

Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, attributes the slowdown partly to a fall in energy sector earnings and partly to weaker growth and margins as higher energy costs and interest rates feed through. Slower growth, high public deficits and elevated energy prices are all expected to weigh. Even so, Bell expects European equities to keep delivering positive returns and to attract continued inflows, particularly from investors outside the region.

Valuations offer less of a cushion than they once did. European stocks still trade at a discount to US peers, but that gap has narrowed to about 14% on a sector-adjusted price-to-earnings basis, from as much as 34%, leaving it roughly in line with history. With the discount smaller and earnings growth slower than elsewhere, Goldman expects European indexes to lag modestly. The Stoxx 600 is already up around 10% this year, a gain that has trailed the much stronger rise in company earnings.

The bank sees several reasons for global investors to keep buying. European markets, notably Switzerland's SMI and Britain's FTSE 100, have held up and in some cases risen as artificial intelligence stocks have sold off, offering diversification. Free cash flow remains relatively high and buybacks strong, while a lighter pipeline of new listings and active mergers are shrinking net equity supply. Goldman already sees investors, especially from the US, adding to European exposure through global funds, even as domestic investors remain cautious.

Energy is the swing factor. Goldman estimates that each 10% rise in Brent crude knocks around 1% off European equity valuations, so the region has the most to gain from relief on energy supply and the most to lose if it does not come. The bank's commodities team expects Brent to fall to $78 a barrel by the end of 2027, from around $91 recently, with European gas prices also declining as suppliers adapt to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Lower energy costs would favour cyclical stocks, consumer discretionary names and Germany's DAX, while energy, defensive and quality stocks, along with the FTSE 100, would be likely to underperform.

Government debt remains a drag. Corporate balance sheets are not stretched, but Bell warns that banks and domestically focused stocks could not escape a broader sovereign risk event. Historically, a 10 basis point widening in the spread between French and German bond yields has coincided with a fall of around 3% in the CAC 40 and 4% in French domestic stocks. Bell considers it too early to return to French domestic stocks and prefers Germany, given relatively low valuations and fiscal spending, along with UK domestic stocks that could benefit if gilt yields and energy prices fall.

Goldman's call is more cautious than some rivals. Deutsche Bank this week forecast the Stoxx 600 at 750 by the end of 2027, roughly 20% higher, though over a slightly longer horizon and on a price rather than total return basis.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Australia trimmed mean CPI jumps to 3.8% in October, keeping further RBA hike risk alive
item.description:
The core beat should support the Australian dollar and push front-end yields higher as traders trim bets on 2027 rate cuts and price in some risk of another hike. December pricing is unlikely to change much, given the weak labour market and the RBA's view that policy is already restrictive. The bigger shift is for the February meeting, which now looks more open. A firmer AUD would ease some imported inflation pressure, while rate-sensitive sectors on the ASX, including property and consumer discretionary, may come under pressure if markets price a longer period of high rates.

---

Data here earlier:

  • AUD jumps: Australia October trimmed mean CPI 3.8% y/y (expected 3.6%, prior 3.6%).

---

Australian core inflation rose further from target in October, leaving a December hold the likeliest outcome but putting further RBA hikes back in play for 2027 and pushing rate-cut hopes further out.

Summary:

  • Trimmed mean CPI rose 3.8% y/y in October, above the 3.6% forecast and up from 3.6%
  • Trimmed mean rose 0.5% m/m, against expectations of 0.3%
  • Headline CPI rose 4.9% y/y (expected 4.7%, prior 4.3%) and 0.5% m/m (expected 0.4%)
  • The weighted median held at 3.4% y/y and rose 0.3% m/m
  • The RBA has raised rates by 125 basis points this year to 4.85%, with inflation well above its 2% to 3% target
  • December is still seen as a hold, but more hikes cannot be ruled out, and the first 2027 decision is due on 9 February

Australia's underlying inflation accelerated more than expected in October, with the Reserve Bank of Australia's preferred trimmed mean measure rising to 3.8% from a year earlier, up from 3.6% in September and above the 3.6% forecast, according to figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. The trimmed mean climbed 0.5% over the month, outpacing expectations of 0.3% and the 0.3% gain the previous month.

Headline inflation also topped forecasts, rising 0.5% in the month to take the annual rate to 4.9%, up from 4.3% and above the 4.7% expected. Higher fuel prices and the unwinding of electricity subsidies had been flagged as the main drivers of the headline increase, but the strength of the core measures points to broader price pressure. The weighted median, another underlying gauge, held at 3.4% year on year, with a 0.3% monthly rise.

The figures challenge the view, widely held ahead of the release, that October would mark the peak in inflation. The RBA's own November forecasts had headline inflation topping out at 4.5%, and the trimmed mean is now further above the bank's 2% to 3% target range than it was a month ago.

The RBA has raised its cash rate by 125 basis points this year, to 4.85%, as inflation stayed well above target. Its November decision was split, with three of nine board members preferring to hold, and the statement dropped its warning that further increases might be needed. A sharp rise in unemployment to 4.9% in October had since reinforced expectations that the tightening cycle was over.

A hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting still looks the most likely outcome, given the weakening labour market and the RBA's assessment that policy is now clearly restrictive. However, with core inflation moving further from target, further rate increases cannot be ruled out. The board's first decision of 2027 is due on 9 February, with two more monthly inflation reports due before then, and those figures are likely to determine whether the October jump proves a one-off or the start of a more persistent trend. Markets that had priced a first rate cut in the second half of 2027 may need to push that timing back.

Reserve Bank of Australia Governor Bullock facing stagflationary pressures.

item.title: Japan services producer prices jump 4.2% in October, firming the case for a BOJ hike
item.description:
A clear beat on services inflation adds weight to December BOJ hike pricing. That should offer the yen some support and nudge short-dated JGB yields higher, especially if upcoming wage data confirms the pass-through. The yen's response may be limited while the Fed is also on a hiking path, which keeps the rate gap with the US wide and USD/JPY elevated. For equities, firmer BOJ expectations are a headwind for rate-sensitive sectors and exporters, while banks stand to benefit from higher margins. The rise in ocean freight costs is a reminder that Middle East shipping disruption is still feeding through to Asian prices.

---

Japanese companies are paying more for each other's services, with freight, leasing and hotel costs pushing the index to a 4.2% annual rise and giving the BOJ another reason to tighten in December.

Summary:

  • Japan's services producer price index rose 4.2% y/y in October, above the 3.6% forecast
  • September's gain was revised to 3.8%
  • Ocean freight, leasing and hotel charges drove the increase
  • The BOJ uses the index to gauge how far firms pass labour costs on to services prices
  • The BOJ's policy rate stands at 1.25% after hikes in June and September
  • Most analysts expect a December hike and another by end-March, with a peak of around 1.75% to 2.0%

Prices that Japanese companies charge each other for services rose at a faster pace than expected in October, adding to evidence that inflation is broadening across the economy and strengthening the case for another Bank of Japan rate increase. The services producer price index climbed 4.2% from a year earlier, well above the 3.6% forecast and up from a revised 3.8% in September, according to Bank of Japan data reported by Reuters.

The rise was driven largely by higher ocean freight costs, leasing fees and hotel charges. The BOJ watches the index closely as a guide to how far firms are passing rising labour costs on to the prices of services, a key link in its assessment of whether inflation is becoming self-sustaining rather than driven mainly by imported costs.

That distinction matters because external pressures remain intense. Stubbornly high energy costs and the rising price of imports, amplified by a weak yen, have kept inflation elevated, and the BOJ has responded by quickening its pace of tightening. It raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, following a hike in June, a much shorter gap between moves than the roughly twice-yearly increases of 2024 and 2025.

Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled that the bank is ready to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from overshooting its 2% target. A firm services reading supports that stance, suggesting price pressure is no longer confined to goods and energy.

Markets and economists are positioned for more. A majority of analysts in a recent poll expect the BOJ to raise rates again in December and follow up with a further increase by the end of March, with many seeing the peak in borrowing costs at around 1.75% to 2.0%.

The December policy meeting is now the focus, with upcoming wage and consumer price data likely to shape the timing. A broad, domestically driven rise in services prices would leave the bank with fewer reasons to wait, particularly with the yen still under pressure.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6559 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBA's Jacobs: five hikes have made policy clearly restrictive, but the squeeze is uneven
item.description:
Jacobs' remarks support the market view that the RBA's tightening cycle is over, with policy now judged restrictive and housing taking the strain. That leans toward a softer Australian dollar and lower front-end yields over time. His point that a higher neutral rate may be blunting policy is a two-sided risk, though: if inflation proves sticky, it could argue against cutting as early as markets hope. Today's October CPI is the immediate test. A firm trimmed mean would strengthen the "tight on paper, less so in practice" reading and could push back pricing for 2027 cuts.

Newswire cut: RBA's David Jacobs says policy is clearly restrictive after five hikes to 4.85%, biting hardest in housing. But low credit spreads and strong business lending blur the picture, and he says a global urge to invest may be lifting the neutral rate.

One-line wrap: The RBA's domestic markets head says five rate rises have made policy clearly restrictive and housing is feeling it, but buoyant credit markets and a possibly higher neutral rate mean the squeeze is less uniform than headline rates suggest.

Summary:

  • RBA's David Jacobs says financial conditions are clearly restrictive after five rate rises this year
  • The expected real cash rate has risen above estimates of the neutral rate, with housing hit hardest
  • Low credit spreads and strong business lending make the degree of restriction harder to judge
  • A global preference to invest rather than save may be lifting the neutral rate, reducing the restraint from any given cash rate
  • Jacobs warns restrictiveness could bite harder if the housing downturn proves larger than expected
  • He says whether policy is tight enough to tame inflation is a matter for the board

Main article: Australian monetary policy is now clearly restrictive after five interest rate increases this year, according to David Jacobs, head of domestic markets at the Reserve Bank of Australia, though he cautioned that the degree of tightness is harder to pin down than the level of rates alone would suggest. Speaking at an event in Sydney on Wednesday, Jacobs said the expected real cash rate had moved above estimates of the neutral rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy, Reuters reported.

Jacobs said the effects were most visible in interest-rate-sensitive parts of the economy, particularly housing. He also flagged a risk that the squeeze could prove stronger than intended, noting that restrictiveness could bite harder if the economic fallout from the housing downturn turns out to be larger than expected.

The picture elsewhere is less clear. Credit spreads remain low and business lending is strong, which Jacobs said makes it difficult to judge how restrictive conditions really are. In his view, the effects of tighter financial conditions are not as even across the economy as the high level of real interest rates might imply.

Part of the explanation, he suggested, may lie outside Australia. A strong global preference to invest rather than save could be lifting the neutral rate, which would reduce the restraint delivered by any given cash rate. If that is the case, a policy setting that looks tight on paper may be exerting less pressure than it appears.

Jacobs stopped short of drawing a policy conclusion, saying that whether the current stance is restrictive enough to bring inflation back to target is a matter for the RBA board.

The RBA has lifted its cash rate to 4.85%, an 18-year high, in its effort to contain inflation. A sharp rise in unemployment, to 4.9% in October, has since led markets to bet that rates have peaked, with a first cut priced for the second half of 2027. The board meets again on 7 and 8 December, when a hold is widely expected. October consumer price data, due later on Wednesday, is the next test, with headline inflation forecast to rise to 4.8%.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: How crypto loans unwind: what a $43.8 million ether sale teaches about leverage
item.description:
BTCS's sale is too small to move ether's price directly. The bigger effect is on how investors view listed crypto treasury firms, whose shares tend to trade as leveraged bets on the coins they hold. BTCS fell nearly 9%. The episode may push investors to look harder at how much other ether-heavy companies have borrowed. Spot ether ETFs are in a run of outflows and bitcoin is below $60,000, so risk appetite across crypto is fragile. Further forced-sale disclosures could hurt sentiment more than they add to supply.

-

A balance sheet that looked well covered on paper was only a 19% ether drop from forced liquidation, and BTCS paid to close that gap before Aave closed it for them.

Summary:

  • BTCS sold about 27,300 ETH on November 20 for $43.8 million and used it all to repay Aave debt, per an 8-K filed November 23.
  • Its Aave borrowing fell to about $10.5 million from an implied $54.3 million.
  • Its November 9 position (about $64.1 million owed against 46,676 ETH) implied a liquidation price of around $1,720. Ether fell near $1,560 on November 20.
  • The company is left with about 24,245 ETH. TheStreet puts its loan-to-value ratio at about 32%.
  • Its DeFi unit, Imperium, has paused its liquidity pool positions, and about $17.9 million of convertible notes are due in 2027.

Nasdaq-listed BTCS sold about 27,300 ETH on November 20 and used the full $43.8 million in proceeds to repay debt on Aave, the decentralised lending protocol, according to a Form 8-K filed with the SEC on November 23. The sale cut its Aave borrowing to roughly $10.5 million. It came as ether briefly fell near $1,560, below a liquidation level that had been estimated from the company's own quarterly filing only days earlier.

The deal is small for the ether market. But it is a clear, documented example of how crypto-backed borrowing works, and of how quickly a comfortable-looking position can become a forced sale.

How an Aave loan works

Aave lends stablecoins against crypto collateral, and every loan is overcollateralised: the borrower must lock up more value than it borrows. Three measures matter.

Loan-to-value (LTV) is the debt divided by the value of the collateral. A $50 loan against $100 of ether is a 50% LTV.

The liquidation threshold is the share of collateral value Aave will count when judging whether a loan is safe. BTCS has said this is generally 80% for ETH.

The health factor combines the two: collateral value multiplied by the liquidation threshold, divided by the debt. Above 1, the loan is safe. Below 1, Aave's smart contracts can sell the borrower's collateral automatically to repay the lender, with no phone call and no negotiation.

The BTCS numbers, worked through

BTCS's quarterly filing showed it owed about $64.1 million on Aave as of November 9. That was backed by 46,676 ETH valued at about $99.3 million, using an ether price of around $2,130. The collateral covered the debt about 1.55 times over, which sounds like a wide margin.

Apply the 80% threshold, though, and the health factor comes out near 1.24. That implies a liquidation price of around $1,720 per ETH, close to CoinDesk's own estimate. In other words, collateral worth 155% of the debt left a price buffer of only about 19%.

Ether then fell roughly 27% from the $2,130 marker to its November 20 low. BTCS had already cut its debt to an implied $54.3 million before that day, which would have lowered its real liquidation line. The company has not disclosed where that line sat. What the filings do show is that it chose to sell rather than wait.

Why sell before the protocol does

A borrower facing a falling health factor has three choices: add collateral, repay debt, or let the protocol liquidate. BTCS held very little cash, reporting about $463,000 at the end of September, so adding collateral meant finding ether it did not have. Liquidation would have meant selling on the protocol's terms, at the worst moment and with a penalty attached.

Selling its own ether to repay the debt let BTCS choose the timing. Chief executive Charles Allen said, according to TheStreet, that the company preferred to cut its Aave borrowing rather than carry the debt through a falling market. The cost is permanent. The average sale price, around $1,600, locks in the loss, and BTCS is left with about 24,245 ETH. "We are a smaller company today," Allen said.

What the sale did to the risk

TheStreet reported the company's loan-to-value ratio at about 32% after the repayment. On that figure, and using the same 80% threshold, ether would need to fall about 60% before the remaining loan neared liquidation. That works out to roughly $690, based on the $1,722 price BTCS used for November 22. This is an illustration rather than a disclosed level, but it shows how much room paying down debt buys.

The trade-off is that the company now has less ether to earn from. Its DeFi unit, Imperium, has temporarily exited its liquidity pool positions. BTCS also still has about $17.9 million of senior secured convertible notes due in May and July 2027. Its shares fell nearly 9%.

Does one forced seller move ether?

Not on its own. The $43.8 million sale is roughly a quarter of 1% of the $17 billion or so in ether traded over 24 hours, according to CoinGecko data. The more useful signal for ETH holders is the pattern. Companies and traders who borrow against ether all face the same arithmetic, and a falling price can push several of them to sell at once. That is how leverage can turn a decline into a sharper one, even when no single seller is large.

The backdrop is already weak. Ether traded around $1,690 on Wednesday in Asia, down roughly 28% over the past month, after a bounce to around $1,840 on November 23 failed to hold. US spot ether ETFs recorded a seventh straight day of net outflows on November 23, according to SoSoValue data, and bitcoin dropped below $60,000 for the first time since July.

What to watch next

The next thing to watch is further disclosure. Another BTCS 8-K showing more sales, or new borrowing, would show whether this was a one-off reset or the start of a longer unwind. The same goes for other listed companies holding ether on borrowed money. Their filings will show how close their collateral sits to the 80% line.

ETF flows are the second marker. A return to inflows while ether holds above its November 20 low would suggest forced selling is easing. Continued outflows alongside new lows would raise the odds that more leveraged holders face the choice BTCS faced.

What could change the reading: if ether recovers quickly, BTCS's sale will look like expensive insurance it never needed. That would not make it the wrong call. A health factor measures how far the price can fall before someone else decides for you, and the cheapest time to act is before that room runs out.

Key terms:

Overcollateralised: a loan backed by collateral worth more than the amount borrowed.

Liquidation threshold: the share of collateral value a lending protocol counts toward a loan's safety.

Health factor: collateral value multiplied by the liquidation threshold, divided by the debt. Below 1, the collateral can be sold automatically.

Form 8-K: a US filing companies use to report major events between quarterly reports.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia triples its oil storage in Japan as Tokyo buys 8m barrels to refill reserves
item.description:
Japan's purchase of up to 8 million barrels is modest against global flows, but it adds a source of committed demand just as oil sells off on surplus fears. Restocking by consumers whose emergency reserves were drawn down this year could put a floor under prompt crude demand. For Saudi Arabia, extra storage in Japan gives it barrels positioned close to Asian buyers, which helps it respond quickly to disruptions and defend market share as Gulf flows recover. If other importers strike similar arrangements, as MUFG expects, the trend would support Middle Eastern exporters' long-term grip on Asian demand.

--

Japan is restocking its emergency reserves with Saudi crude and giving Riyadh three times more room to store oil on Japanese soil, a sign that this year's Gulf disruptions are pushing buyers and sellers toward deeper supply partnerships.

Summary:

  • Japan will buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its strategic petroleum reserve
  • Saudi Arabia gains access to a further 16 million barrels of storage in Japan, on top of 8 million already available
  • Saudi Arabia supplied 42% of Japan's crude imports in 2025, with the UAE close behind at 41%
  • The Middle East accounted for 93% of Japan's total oil imports
  • The deal secures supply for Japan and a reliable outlet for Saudi exports
  • MUFG expects more storage deals and wider access for Gulf exporters after this year's disruptions

Japan and Saudi Arabia have agreed a strategic oil storage arrangement that will see Tokyo buy up to 8 million barrels of Saudi crude to refill its petroleum reserve, while Riyadh gains significantly more space to store oil on Japanese soil. Under the deal, Saudi Arabia will have access to a further 16 million barrels of storage capacity in Japan, adding to the 8 million barrels it already had and tripling its total to 24 million barrels, according to a note from MUFG.

The agreement reflects Japan's heavy dependence on Gulf supply. Saudi Arabia was Japan's largest source of crude imports in 2025, accounting for 42% of the total, with the United Arab Emirates close behind at 41%. Overall, oil from the Middle East made up 93% of Japan's imports, leaving the country among the most exposed of the major consumers to disruption in the region.

That exposure has been tested this year, as conflict in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed consumer nations to draw on emergency stocks. Refilling those reserves is now a priority for importers, and long-term supply relationships offer a way to rebuild them with greater certainty.

The benefits run both ways. For Japan, a larger and more durable link with its biggest supplier helps secure access to crude in a crisis. For Saudi Arabia, storage in Japan provides a reliable destination for its exports and positions barrels close to major Asian buyers, allowing quicker deliveries when supply chains are strained elsewhere.

MUFG expects the model to spread. It sees scope for existing storage facilities to be expanded, and for Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern exporters to secure storage access in a wider range of countries, as both producers and consumers look to guard against a repeat of this year's disruption. With oil prices under pressure from expectations of a looming surplus, such arrangements could also help Gulf exporters lock in demand as their shipments recover. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
